Anthropic’s Backers Have Another Significant Bet: Americans Staying Renters

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s stock market debut on Thursday is expected to value the artificial intelligence company at $1.5 trillion, putting some of Wall Street’s biggest investment firms in line to cash in from its rapid rise.
  • It has been revealed that in its pitch to investors, the maker of Claude offers a vision far grander than the 2,800 millionaires the IPO is expected to mint.
  • But some of its backers are making another bet on a future where renting dominates the housing market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s stock market debut on Thursday is expected to value the artificial intelligence company at $1.5 trillion, putting some of Wall Street’s biggest investment firms in line to cash in from its rapid rise.

It has been revealed that in its pitch to investors, the maker of Claude offers a vision far grander than the 2,800 millionaires the IPO is expected to mint. AI, it notes, could “significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.”.

But some of its backers are making another bet on a future where renting dominates the housing market.

Among them are Blackstone and Brookfield, two investment giants whose portfolios extend from emerging technologies to the nation's housing stock.

“Amidst continued macroeconomic uncertainty, we believe rental housing is the number one thing you want to own,” reads a 2025 shareholder upgrade from Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust, known as BREIT.

Under a heading touting Blackstone Real Estate’s “Best Ideas,” the fund pointed to record homeownership costs, sluggish construction, and a national shortage of 4 million to 5 million homes. It called those conditions “powerful tailwinds” for its rental housing investments.

To housing advocates, though, those tailwinds are precisely the headwinds they’re working to reverse, states Jordan Ash, housing director at the nonprofit watchdog Private Equity Stakeholder Project.

The investment thesis anticipates a future in which “there are many more people who are just going to be renters for life,” Ash tells Realtor.com®.

Sources indicate that “The renter is not their customer,” he claims of large private equity landlords. “They're accountable to their investors.”.

And now, the rental market is showing signs of turning in those investors’ favor.

Median asking rents rose 0.1% in October—the first annual increase since June 2023—across the 50 largest metros, according to Realtor.com research. The increase was small, but it came as the apartment construction boom that helped hold rents down began to fade.

Meanwhile, households that might otherwise leave the rental market face a steep price for becoming homeowners.

Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, roughly double their 3.69% level in October 2019, notes Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu.

Recent findings suggest that “Elevated mortgage rates are one of the key barriers to homeownership, because they significantly raise the monthly cost of buying,” she explains. Higher ownership expenses have added to the burden.

That financial hurdle is apparent in Dallas–Fort Worth, TX, where Blackstone owns rental homes through Tricon, the operator it acquired in 2024.

Across the metro, the median monthly cost of buying a starter home was $2,741 in October, compared with $1,471 to rent, according to data from Realtor.com. That means making the leap to homeownership would involve finding an additional $1,270 in the monthly budget—after also coming up with a down payment.

It's easy to understand the bet then—with a gap that wide, who would ever be able to afford the jump?

Recent findings suggest that washington has tried to make that leap easier by limiting buyers’ competition from Wall Street. Following President Donald Trump’s January executive order, Congress enacted restrictions on additional single-family home purchases by institutional investors controlling at least 350 such homes. The ban takes effect on Jan. 7, 2027, with exceptions that include qualifying build-to-rent projects.

It has been revealed that but limiting competition from investors does not, by itself, close the monthly gap between renting and owning. And while that gap gives households a reason to keep renting, BREIT expects declining construction to give landlords more room to raise rents.

Sources indicate that “Ultimately, lower supply should support rent growth and real estate values over time,” the fund wrote in its Nov. 4 shareholder patch, which did not address the institutional investor ban.

Of course, that outcome isn’t assured. Although the multifamily construction pipeline has shrunk from its peak, it remains large by pre-pandemic standards, Xu states. Projects already underway could continue giving tenants more options.

Even so, “If new multifamily deliveries cannot keep pace with rental demand, we expect rents to rise,” she says.

But even buying a home doesn't always end the relationship with a landlord.

Ash points to Brookfield’s acquisition of YES Communities, an operator of manufactured-home communities where residents can own their houses while paying rent for the land beneath them.

Recent findings suggest that residents’ complaints about rising costs and neglected maintenance predated Brookfield’s purchase. And as the deal approached, some appealed directly to pension funds invested with the firm, seeking assurances that a newly introduced owner would improve their circumstances.

“The rent just keeps going up, but no improvements have been made,” Michigan resident Abbie Pedrotte told University of California regents, according to Ash’s reporting.

By October, those concerns had reached Congress.

In an Oct. 13 letter, Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) and two colleagues pressed Brookfield about its looks. They asked whether it intended to raise home and lot rents by more than 3% annually and whether it would cooperate with residents seeking to purchase their parks. Written answers were requested by Nov. 20.

For its part, Brookfield’s published strategy calls for increasing resident homeownership and expanding tenant programs to “boost operating income and retention.” Owning the house can give a resident a stake in the community while preserving the landlord’s income from the land.

In a recent development, “We own the appreciating part of real estate. It’s fantastic,” Lowell Baron, CEO of Brookfield’s real estate business, told investors in September.

Some of the firms betting on continued demand for rentals are also financing a construction boom of their own.

BREIT had deployed more than $9 billion into data center developments in 2026 by its November shareholder revision, helping expand the infrastructure supporting AI and cloud computing.

Blackstone has already identified a potential cost for other real estate—including homebuilding.

On its October earnings call, President Jon Gray remarked rising construction costs and limited latest supply were being intensified by higher interest rates and “crowding out from the AI infrastructure build.”.

A construction industry survey offers evidence of that competition. Among firms reporting on data center projects’ workforce effects, 58% cited increased competition for skilled workers, while 49% reported greater wage pressure, according to the 2026 AGC/NCCER Workforce Survey.

Xu cautions against treating those findings as a measure of the impact on homebuilding.

“The survey points to labor pressure where data centers are concentrated, but it does not isolate AI investment from factors like immigration enforcement and tariffs, nor does it directly measure residential construction costs,” she explains.

And to their credit, the private equity firms are also moving to help finance additional housing. Blackstone launched a homebuilder lending platform in May that it expects to support more than 50,000 new for-sale homes annually.

Buying existing homes changes ownership without adding to the housing stock, Xu explains.

“Financing latest construction, by contrast, increases the stock, which is the key to expanding supply and improving affordability for both groups,” she states.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s backers have capital to help build the future they describe. Households waiting for a more affordable home need some of that future to include them.

UPDATED 16:38 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Sources indicate that U.S. authorities don’t believe that the recent outages at federal agencies and top tech firms were caused by cyberattacks.

According to recent reports, the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, Apple Inc. and Microsoft Corp. were among the affected organizations. All four said that their systems were disrupted by technical problems rather than hackers. Experts noted that artificial intelligence models’ ability to find software bugs has made patching more complicated, which may increase the risk of outages.

Recent findings suggest that the first major service disruption hit Exchange Online on Thursday. The Microsoft-operated email service went offline for nearly a day, which left 450 million people without access to their inboxes. The company attributed the downtime to two separate bugs in the software that powers its network. The first one went undetected for three months, while the other cropped up a day before the outage.

According to recent reports, the FAA experienced a network disruption of its own on Friday. An matter with a router at the agency’s El Dorado, Arkansas campus disrupted aircraft communications and radar data feeds. The outage led to more than 12,000 flight cancellations.

United Airlines reported a fairly extensive, but brief infrastructure disruption a few days later. The problem took several of the carrier’s pilot-facing applications offline for 30 minutes. Fewer than 150 flights were affected.

Yet another high-profile network outage occurred on Tuesday, this time at the U.S. National Security Agency. A technical problem cropped up in NSANet, an internal network that agency staff use to exchange classified information. The cause of the outage and its duration were not specified. However, officials did tell NBC the disruption wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.

U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that point in a Tuesday interview. He added that officials have “looked very closely” into the other outages that occurred over the past week and ruled out cyberattacks as the cause. According to Clayton, authorities believe that the disruptions occurred because companies are patching vulnerabilities “on much larger scale” than before.

Frontier AI models have found thousands of software vulnerabilities over the past few months. That accelerated pace of discovery is creating more work for administrators, who have to roll out patches more frequently than before. The less time there is to prepare a patch, the greater the risk of human error.

“As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and development cycles, pressure is mounting on companies to deploy fixes rapidly, often without fully understanding how those changes will affect interconnected systems, “ said Prince Kohli, the chief executive officer of software testing provider Sauce Labs Inc. “The only way to prevent these problems is continuous testing and release validation in their development processes, even more so for critical software updates.”.

It has been revealed that apple and Workday Inc. are also among the companies that have experienced outages in recent days. Separately, several financial services temporarily became unavailable because of an issue with one of JPMorgan Chase’s on-premises systems. All the incidents have been resolved.

Tech Report: A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he remarked.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

In a recent development, sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Industry observers note that athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” mentioned Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively latest sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

According to recent reports, you have to be patient when working with athletes, he stated, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

According to recent reports, what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he mentioned.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

It has been revealed that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

According to recent reports, but that can be a long road. Sangaré noted it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

It has been revealed that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré remarked; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

Industry News: Anthropic’s Blockbuster IPO Set To Spark a Upcoming San Francisco Housing Frenzy: ‘Expect More All-Cash Offers’ and Bidding Wars

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate agents in San Francisco are bracing for further acceleration of the housing market as Anthropic makes an initial public offering at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Bay Area has been a hot spot for newly wealthy AI trendsetters in recent years, rebuilding a market that was left hurting during the COVID-19 pandemic as tech offices emptied.
  • Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO went live on Thursday, marking one of the largest public-market debuts in history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate agents in San Francisco are bracing for further acceleration of the housing market as Anthropic makes an initial public offering at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion.

Recent findings suggest that the Bay Area has been a hot spot for newly wealthy AI trendsetters in recent years, rebuilding a market that was left hurting during the COVID-19 pandemic as tech offices emptied. With major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic planting roots in San Francisco, the housing market has grown competitive, leading what some real estate agents are calling a “mansion shortage.”.

Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO went live on Thursday, marking one of the largest public-market debuts in history.

In a recent development, the Claude developer, which will trade under the ticker ANT, initially stated it planned to price shares at between $70 and $78, which would value the manufacturer at between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Late Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported the company planned to debut at $83 per share, taking the valuation to $1.5 trillion.

In addition to the public offering, Anthropic is set to receive an extra $26 billion in a private placement sale of shares to several other major tech companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and more, according to Yahoo Finance.

While employees and insiders won't see cash in hand until after a significant lockup period, the debut could give many early shareholders the confidence to move forward with real estate purchases.

Sources indicate that “Confidence may change before purchasing power does. There are lockup periods, taxes, and individual circumstances to consider, so I wouldn’t expect everyone to start buying houses the following week,” San Francisco real estate agent and founder of Vivre Real Estate, Danielle Lazier, tells Realtor.com®. “But the anticipation has already motivated some buyers to act because they’re concerned about competing with more AI money later.”.

Recent findings suggest that this will not be the first IPO debut that Lazier has worked through, so she knows how the influx of confidence and wealth can push people toward real estate investments. Even tech companies that hit major milestones without going public can lead to major shifts in local spending.

“Having worked here through Google, Facebook, and other IPOs, I’ve seen how that wealth can move into housing as people diversify and make longer-term prepares,” claims Lazier. “OpenAI hasn’t gone public, but its private stock sales have already helped employees buy homes.”.

The AI boom has already significantly reshaped the housing market in the Bay Area. Realtor.com research found that elevated down payments in the Bay Area, when compared to key comparison markets like Miami, Latest York City, and Austin, TX, are evidence of the impact of AI wealth.

The study captured baseline down payment numbers from 2020 to 2022, when AI hadn’t yet taken hold and mortgage rates hadn’t spiked. When mortgage rates peaked in 2023 and buyers put more money down if able, down payments within the luxury home market rose between 3 and 8 percentage points in all four metros.

It has been revealed that in the 2024–25 period, mortgage rates had eased, but the AI boom was in full swing. Down payments in Miami, New York City, and Austin all met or dropped below their pre-rate-shock level, but buyers in the Bay Area continued to put 6.6 percentage points more down to buy a home, showing clear evidence that AI equity had found its way into pockets and into real estate.

By 2026, the median down payment in counties considered to be AI hubs, including San Francisco, Santa Clara, and San Mateo, reached 25%, while median down payment in nearby nonhub counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, and Marin remained at 20%.

When applied to the AI-hub group’s median listing price of about $1.33 million, that 5-percentage-point difference translates to $61,180 in additional down payment, according to Realtor.com data.

The influx of new wealth has been compounded by a limited number of desirable homes, making the market fiercely competitive.

It has been revealed that “Additional purchasing power is competing for a limited resource. We have very few spacious, finished homes with practical layouts in desirable location,” states Lazier. “Having the money to renovate doesn’t mean having the time or interest to manage a San Francisco construction project.”.

Homes with completed renovations, outdoor space, views, and privacy draw the most interest. Lazier mentions that she expects listings like 2770 Broadway, which hit the market last week as the city’s most expensive listing of 2026, to be ones to watch.

The stunning seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home hits all the marks: a beautiful view of the San Francisco Bay, a sport court in the back, and a 2007 renovation that combines its classic architecture with functional modern living.

It also comes with a $35 million asking price.

More competitive buyers could mean more bidding wars, but not every listing should expect that, according to Cameron Walker of Clever Real Estate.

“Expect more all-cash offers, shorter time on the market, and more bidding wars,” Walker tells Realtor.com. “But a hot market doesn’t mean everyone’s house will get overbid offers. The newly rich are discerning homebuyers, so expect well-priced houses to get multiple offers and overpriced houses to languish.”.

Not everyone will be going after massive estates with flashy price tags. A comfortable home close to company offices and existing connections will see high demand.

Neighborhoods such as Noe Valley, Pacific Heights, Presidio Heights, and Cole Valley are ones to watch following Anthropic’s debut, according to Walker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the early ’90s, I worked in Wells Fargo Bank’s real estate workout group in Southern California. The aerospace collapse was crushing the local economy; Los Angeles County alone lost 400,000 jobs. Roughly 25% of WFB’s assets were in commercial real estate (including homebuilding), and another 25% in home mortgages, mostly in California. That was half the bank. Writing off loans and walking away to clean up the books wasn’t an option; we lacked the capital. So we fought for every penny.

According to recent reports, we asked for re-margins early on, short-term extensions and collected from borrowers before they ran out of money. We pursued personal guarantees and were willing to fight for them. I realize it is not what an audience of builders wants to hear, but everyone fights to survive.

Bank of America was in a different position. It had less real estate concentration and wanted to expand by buying distressed banks, but it couldn’t until regulators were convinced it had moved past its own problems. So BofA cut deals or foreclosed, cleaning house. Its real estate recovery rate was far lower than ours. That doesn’t mean BofA was wrong. It simply had different incentives.

Everyone knows Charlie Munger’s line, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”.

Industry observers note that we tend to apply it to individuals. But the coming year will be driven largely by company incentives. If you’re a builder, understanding the incentives of the companies across the table may be the most valuable market intelligence you can gather.

Why the coming year? As I’ve said before, I’m not a major fan of short-term market projections. Over longer time spans, demographics, the fundamental balance of supply and demand, and affordability play out; they’re directionally predictable, if not precise. The short term has so many unforeseeable temporary factors that it can, paradoxically, be harder to call. Strategy is for the long term; in the short run, it’s mostly tactics, adapting to what’s in front of you. But caution about predicting short-term conditions is different from dismissing contingency planning.

Housing market conditions have clearly deteriorated. Whatever the cause (war, politics, rising rates or all of the above), I suspect we never had the correction we should have after rates spiked in ’22. A frozen-in-place resale market and the effectiveness of rate buydowns made the following years difficult, but less so than many of us expected.

One of the most intriguing aspects is that I can’t recall a more difficult period in homebuilding (to be clear, I’ve been through far worse, twice) that had so little impact on the land market. The reason was the belief that land was in such short supply that builders couldn’t afford to give up what they had and would need to buy more. Builders weren’t staying in current deals because they necessarily made sense, nor were they buying new ones because they liked the prices.

The attitude was: what’s the alternative?

Recent findings suggest that that belief rested on two assumptions. First, that today’s weakness is a short-term problem: the rate shock would wear off, and buying would pick up. Second, that long-term fundamentals hadn’t changed, so demand would rebound and buoy prices. Either could prove true, but I’m skeptical. As I’ve written over the past year, future demand looks weak relative to the past, not a temporary dip but the start of a regime change. Once that becomes conventional wisdom, why would builders feel the need to control six to seven years of lots? Remember when three to four was considered plenty? Why won’t that be the case again?

I think 2027 is the year land prices will correct, not just terms but real prices. It’s current economics meeting a dawning recognition that the future will need fewer lots. Beyond a few year-end closings, not much will happen in the rest of 2026, and some will wait to see whether a magic spring rebound arrives. But over the last few months, we’ve seen a sharp downgrade in builder expectations for next year. Few expect things to improve soon.

According to recent reports, the public builders reinforce this. Many are eliminating forecasts or revising unit counts downward. Much like the difference between making a dollar and losing a dollar, which is much bigger than two dollars, once a builder admits it won’t be growing, it becomes much easier to walk from some positions. Once that threshold is crossed, Wall Street cares far less whether a builder shrinks 2% or 6%.

Reasonable people can differ on this; there are multiple paths forward. But I think the odds are high enough to warrant contingency planning. If I’m right, what happens?

According to recent reports, to start, many land bankers (not the old vets, but the newcomers) will learn they weren’t offering a credit product. Like it or not, they’re in real estate and have taken real estate risk. Too many fundamentals in that business were stretched on the belief that big builders wouldn’t walk en masse.

Expect meaningful re-trades, not just extensions. Meanwhile, land sellers will hear builders say they have options and don’t need to rush: “We’ll pay less and take them down on a rolling schedule with a 3% annual escalator. We can’t pay a land banker 10% to hold them; the margin’s too thin.”.

According to recent reports, that’s where incentives come in. How each negotiation goes will depend heavily on the incentives of the companies involved, and each company has multiple layers. Using land bankers as an example, here are a few questions worth addressing.

Industry observers note that how are their asset management fees calculated and collected? As a percentage of revenue, assets (write-downs matter), or cost? Are they amortized over the deal’s life, or literally eat-what-you-kill, paid at closing? Last cycle, it wasn’t uncommon for equity funds to earn asset management fees based on revenue, with half taken up front and the rest amortized over the deal’s projected life.

Industry observers note that when deals stretched out, and total revenue fell, the fee shrank and had to last longer. Once it was used up, it was used up, and a manager could be left without enough fee income to run the business but still obligated to manage the assets. That argues for resolving deals. But many of those structures also triggered a true-up at close-out, which argues for delaying resolution. Which pressure drives a given manager? It depends, and that’s exactly why you need to know.

Is their profit from fees or from promotes? A manager who relies on asset management fees will protect them. A manager focused on promotes, with good profits already built up in a tranche, may prefer to resolve an asset quickly, even at a loss, rather than let the overall IRR erode further.

It has been revealed that millrose Properties is an interesting case. Its external manager, Kennedy Lewis (KL), is paid a fee based on the vehicle’s tangible assets rather than on performance, and Millrose is permanent capital with no fund life to force a resolution. That structure rewards keeping the asset base intact; a sale shrinks it, and so does a write-down. I can’t know how KL will respond, and there are counterweights, since Millrose is a public REIT with a dividend and a stock price to consider.

But if I were betting, I’d expect the fee base to weigh heavily. If conditions worsen, few builders will be seeking latest land banking, so raising more capital matters less until a recovery brings new deals. One way to keep assets on the books would be to lower option fees and ease takedown terms to keep builders in contract, even at weak returns. A more classic fund structure, by contrast, might push a manager toward resolution rather than managing assets for little or no fee.

According to recent reports, similar dynamics will play out among land sellers. Traditionally, well-capitalized sellers are reluctant to cut prices at first. Doing so immediately crushes expected returns, and the weakness might prove temporary. But at some point, it becomes clear it isn’t temporary, and the concern shifts from return on capital to return of capital.

For fund-backed sellers, the next fundraising effort makes the difference between “we’ve never lost money on a deal” and “we’ve never lost more than 5% on a deal” stark. They don’t read the same in a pitch book. So structures that aren’t ideal from a return perspective get more attention: a lower lot price in exchange for a meaningful true-up or profit participation, with little to no deposit and very soft takedowns. These structures keep open the possibility of at least recovering capital.

How do you learn all this? Ask. Some won’t tell you, but more will than you’d expect. Your counterpart has their own pressures and concerns, and a gentle question can yield a lot of information. Ask before you’re in a workout. If you’re buying, ask what their key motivations are and listen carefully to their answers. In effect, you’re trying to determine whether you’re dealing with a Wells Fargo or a Bank of America.

In a recent development, so, what’s the point of these speculations? Just a reminder that we stand a decent chance of 2027 being the year of negotiations. Understanding the incentive structures of those on the other side of the table may be your most notable piece of market intelligence.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

Industry observers note that zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

According to recent reports, october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

It has been revealed that the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a newly introduced transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

It has been revealed that the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

According to recent reports, ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Industry observers note that as of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

In a recent development, small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

According to recent reports, in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Customers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

It has been revealed that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

It has been revealed that the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

In a recent development, brandt's chart reveals Bitcoin forming a left shoulder, a higher peak representing the head, and a lower right shoulder. The cryptocurrency is now testing the neckline of this potential bearish formation, located around the $60,000 to $65,000 region.

Recent findings suggest that however, Brandt has not declared the pattern complete. His warning remains conditional on whether the formation proves to be a legitimate head-and-shoulders top.

The downturn accelerated on Nov. 13, when Bitcoin fell below the psychologically crucial $70,000 level for the first time since August.

Latest Update: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no.
  • According to recent reports, when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

According to recent reports, when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

According to recent reports, expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer stated yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

It has been revealed that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Recent findings suggest that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It has been revealed that it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

In a recent development, when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Industry observers note that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Recent findings suggest that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

In a recent development, listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

According to recent reports, so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

Sources indicate that “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Industry observers note that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc.
  • The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations.
  • The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:13 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. today confirmed that it has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence model training and inference startup Applied Compute Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.

The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations. Shares of Palo Alto Networks rose more than 8% in late trading, adding to a gain of nearly 10% during the regular session.

The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter. Once the deal closes, Applied Compute co-founder and Chief Executive Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, with the startup’s research team also joining the tech giant.

Founded in 2025 by former OpenAI Group PBC researchers Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, Applied Compute offers a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models. The platform is designed to make it easier for companies to train, serve and improve their own models, with an autoscaling inference engine and a model router called Shift-1 also included.

In a recent development, applied Compute raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier this month in a round led by Elad Gil, with Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures and HubSpot Ventures also participating. At the time, the manufacturer said that its annualized recurring revenue had topped $100 million. Notable customers include Microsoft Corp. and DoorDash Inc. Coming into its acquisition, Applied Compute had raised more than $500 million in total.

Palo Alto Networks is pitching the deal as a bet that enterprise AI will be hybrid, as a large share of companies run open-weight models tuned to their own data. According to the tech giant, no large provider is right now delivering those models securely. With Applied Compute, enterprises will be able to train and deploy open-weight models with security built in, either in the public cloud or in sovereign environments.

It has been revealed that “Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Chairman and Chief Executive Nikesh Arora mentioned. “Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we’ve seen, and its research team is exceptional.”.

The deal came on the same day Palo Alto Networks reported what Arora called a record first quarter. For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, the organization reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.05, up from 93 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 97 cents per share on revenue of $3.31 billion.

Recent findings suggest that next-generation security annual recurring revenue grew 66% from a year earlier, to $9.73 billion. Remaining performance obligations rose 35%, to $21 billion. Helped by a tax benefit of $457 million, net income on an unadjusted basis came to $482 million, up from $334 million in the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Dipak Golechha stated that given the current threat environment and the demand ahead, the organization is “materially raising” its full-year guidance.

According to recent reports, for its fiscal second quarter, Palo Alto Networks expects adjusted earnings per share of $1.01 to $1.03 on revenue of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion. Full-year revenue is now forecast at $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up from the $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion guided in September, with adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share ahead of the $4.18 expected by analysts polled by FactSet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newrez agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement broad mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) that the tech giant engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.
  • The consent order, which stems from a multiyear servicing investigation, lands below the $4.175 million civil penalty sought earlier this year by DFI in a statement of charges, but it still represents a significant financial and operational hit for the nonbank servicer.
  • In a recent development, newrez does not admit or deny any wrongdoing under the agreement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newrez agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement broad mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) that the tech giant engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

The consent order, which stems from a multiyear servicing investigation, lands below the $4.175 million civil penalty sought earlier this year by DFI in a statement of charges, but it still represents a significant financial and operational hit for the nonbank servicer.

In a recent development, newrez does not admit or deny any wrongdoing under the agreement. A manufacturer spokesperson told HousingWire the company is “pleased to have resolved this matter.”.

“The underlying examination resulted in limited findings, most of which had already been addressed by Newrez. The agreement, which includes no admission of wrongdoing, credits Newrez for several investments made to enhance its operations. We remain committed to supporting homeowners and meeting the high standards they expect,” the spokesperson said.

In a recent development, under the order, Newrez must pay $2.5 million to DFI, plus at least $500,000 earmarked for consumer remediation and technology and system upgrades. The company also owes an investigation fee of $14,888.90 to cover the agency’s staff time.

Sources indicate that the case grew out of more than 125 consumer complaints to DFI, including allegations of unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting at least 29 borrowers. Regulators also cited failures to maintain and service escrow accounts for at least 71 loans to Washington residents.

Earlier charges alleged servicing breakdowns in Washington from 2021 to 2026. These included loan boarding errors that caused private mortgage insurance and escrow problems, misapplied payments, problems with escrow and force‑placed insurance, inaccurate information during foreclosure mediation, faulty statements, and overdue responses to both borrowers and the regulator.

According to recent reports, in addition to the monetary obligations, the consent order requires Newrez to undertake affirmative actions across its servicing platform. The company must tighten loan onboarding processes, overhaul core servicing functions, and improve controls over escrow and insurance handling, among other changes. Newrez has to demonstrate to DFI that these corrective actions are complete within 30 days of the order’s effective date.

“Washington state mortgage servicing laws exist to ensure homeowners are treated fairly and that their loans are serviced properly,” DFI Director Charlie Clark said in a statement. “DFI will take action to hold mortgage servicers accountable and will order affirmative action needed to protect Washington homeowners.”.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont mentioned in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon mentioned in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Sources indicate that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Recent findings suggest that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an vital step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Industry observers note that inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

Industry observers note that the solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker stated workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

It has been revealed that tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really vital component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Tech Report: Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that national housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million).
  • Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low.

Recent findings suggest that national housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000.

Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum.

“Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units,” according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington.

The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where upcoming home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023.

Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million.

Industry observers note that “Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming mentioned in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.”.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400.

Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline.

“Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he stated.

According to recent reports, the stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025.

Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year.

Industry observers note that year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers.

The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely.

Zillow Senior Economist Kenny Lee noted that the slowdown in single-family starts and permits indicates that homebuilders may be preparing for a relatively weak spring selling season.

“While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane,” Lee explained.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.
  • The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg, Reuters and the Financial Times, is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.
  • If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:50 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg, Reuters and the Financial Times, is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.

If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can.

Industry observers note that the listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks, including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies.

Sources indicate that some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. For instance, both Amazon.com Inc. and Google LLC have sizable stakes in the tech giant, and others including Microsoft Corp., Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. have invested billions into its IPO. Meanwhile, the company is one of the biggest buyers of AI chips from those firms.

“If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei (pictured) remarked in a roadshow video last week. “We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time.”.

Anthropic has been surrounded by immense hype and equally sizable controversy, generating billions of dollars in revenue while raising even more, and sparking serious concerns over the safety of the technology it has pioneered. Amodei has emerged as one of the biggest sources of the numerous doomsday stories surrounding AI, writing essays and repeatedly warning anyone who will listen of the dangers of humans losing control. In addition, he has attracted the ire of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after refusing to let the Pentagon do as it pleases with the manufacturer’s tools.

“If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” Amodei wrote in a viral essay in September.

Sources indicate that industry analyst Dan Ives told the New York Post that most investors view Amodei’s comments as “background noise” relative to the growth opportunity Anthropic has as one of the perceived leaders in frontier model development. “It’s a white-knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he said.

Sources indicate that going forward, Amodei and his team will try to defy a stock market that has looked increasingly volatile this year. But even if they fail, they will walk away from this as incredibly rich men, with some reports suggesting that he and his six co-founders could each earn around $18 billion from today’s sale.

“Anthropic’s IPO will test just how much value frontier AI companies can capture as the industry moves from building increasingly capable models to putting them to work,” DatologyAI Inc. CEO Ari Morcos told SiliconANGLE.

Industry observers note that wall Street anticipates massive growth for the firm in the coming years. Anthropic has been engaged in a titanic struggle with OpenAI Group PBC and Google LLC to develop the best AI models and recruit enterprise customers, and it appears to be winning, at least for now. It has enjoyed a rapid rise this year driven by the success of its popular AI coding tool Claude Code.

According to its IPO prospectus, it generated revenue of $33.24 billion in the nine month period ending Sept. 30, up about 1,200% from the same period one year earlier. During that period, it recorded a staggering $104 billion net loss, though most of that was the result of a change in the value of convertible notes issues to investors and its derivative liabilities, the Financial Times said. Over the same stretch in 2025, Anthropic’s total losses came to $25.1 billion.

In a recent amendment to its IPO filing, the company noted it had achieved a revenue run-rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the prior month.

Regarding projections, some analysts have forecast Anthropic’s revenue to hit $53 billion by the end of its fiscal year, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in fiscal 2027 and between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028.

Industry observers note that anthropic’s rival OpenAI had originally hoped to beat it to the public markets, but its founder and CEO Sam Altman later delayed its listing. Though it has confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, it’s not expected to make its market debut until sometime next year.

“Anthropic’s IPO is going to be the newly introduced bellwether for the AI industry and it could spark a revival if it gets off to a good start,” said Holger Mueller of Constellation Research. “The long-term promise centers on Anthropic’s enterprise workloads and the stickiness of those workloads. But remember that things move very fast in AI an successful 2026 IPO for Anthropic will by no means provide any guarantees for a successful OpenAI IPO next year.”.

Family Found Dead in Foreclosed Home Survived Months Longer Than Previously Thought

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New evidence suggests that at least one member of a family found dead inside a foreclosed-upon Connecticut home survived longer than previously thought—paving the way for transfer of title to a new owner.
  • In a recent development, the bizarre case hinges upon whether the home's owners died before or after the foreclosure was recorded.
  • In a recent development, edward Marchion stumbled into the mystery in June, when he purchased 7 Stanwich Lane, a four-bedroom, 3-bathroom home in Burlington, CT, in a foreclosure auction for $525,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New evidence suggests that at least one member of a family found dead inside a foreclosed-upon Connecticut home survived longer than previously thought—paving the way for transfer of title to a new owner.

In a recent development, the bizarre case hinges upon whether the home's owners died before or after the foreclosure was recorded. If the owners were already dead at the time of the filing, the foreclosure may be deemed illegitimate, and a search for rightful heirs would begin.

In a recent development, edward Marchion stumbled into the mystery in June, when he purchased 7 Stanwich Lane, a four-bedroom, 3-bathroom home in Burlington, CT, in a foreclosure auction for $525,000. The 2,800-square-foot home sits on more than 2 acres and comes with a hot tub, patio, and deck, according to the listing.

A few days after placing the winning bid, Marchion finally entered the property and came across a grisly sight. The skeletal remains of the property’s previous owners, Sally Anne Cash and Paul Cash, and their adult son Brian Cash, were found inside.

Marchion then asked a judge to halt the closing on the property to determine the timeline of the Cashs’ deaths.

According to recent reports, in a July 2 filing in the state Supreme Court, Marchion’s lawyer John C. Lewis III asked the court to delay closing until the Connecticut State Police could determine whether the Cash family died before or after the foreclosure action.

"From a title perspective, unless it can be determined that the Defendants were alive on the date the lis pendens was recorded (August 6, 2025), then the foreclosure action is defective," wrote Lewis.

Now, months later, fresh evidence from the family’s probate attorney and state medical examiner’s office reveals that the family’s deaths likely took place long after the foreclosure paperwork was filed, paving the way for Marchion to receive title to the home.

It has been revealed that paul and Sally Ann Cash purchased 7 Stanwich Lane in 2019. At the time, they took out a $385,000 mortgage on the property. But court records filed by their mortgage servicer revealed that the couple stopped making monthly mortgage payments in December 2024. Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing filed a notice of foreclosure on the property on August 6, 2025.

Sources indicate that when police entered the property this past June, they discovered Paul and Sally Ann in a second-floor bedroom and Brian Cash in a bedroom above the garage. All three were found in sleeping bags and wearing multiple layers of clothing.

The home was packed with clutter and garbage bags, but authorities noted the only food found in the house was powdered milk.

The family was known to have been extremely reclusive and the home’s interior reflected prolonged isolation and deprivation.

The exact cause of death is still being investigated, though authorities believe that either malnutrition or hypothermia were factors.

In late October, Shellpoint attorney Christopher Throgmartin filed a petition to request that proceeds from the sale of the property to Marchion be used to pay outstanding property taxes that accrued while the investigation was taking place. His petition also requested that Marchion be able to access the property in order to winterize and secure it at is own expense.

Two days later, the surviving relatives of the Cashes signed documents waiving their rights to 7 Stanwich Lane, further paving the way for the sale to Marchion to move forward.

Then, in an affidavit filed on November 10, Connecticut State Medical Examiner Dr. Mary Kate Schwerdt testified, “The condition of [Sally Ann Cash’s] internal organs, and the level of decomposition is consistent with a death that occurred after August 6, 2025.”.

Dr. Melissa Pasquale, who completed the autopsy of Brian Cash, testified that he also died sometime after August 6, 2025. The Medical Examiner’s office believes that Paul Cash died first.

Mary Anne Charron, the probate lawyer appointed as estate examiner for Sally Ann and Brian Cash by the Farmington Regional Probate Court, filed an affidavit stating that “In the course of the investigation, I discovered numerous electronic devices, including multiple laptops, flash drives, hard drives, several phones, a camera, as well as thousands of writings which appear to be journal entries, many of which include dates and time of entry.”.

Industry observers note that charron stated she found entries believed to be Sally Ann’s, dated August, September, October, and November 2025. She also found outgoing text messages dated from September and October 2025. The last known phone activity Charron documented was dated December 16, 2025, roughly a year after the Cashes stopped paying their mortgage.

"Based on the dates of the journal entries, text chains and screenshots on cell phones, as well as correspondence with the Medical Examiner regarding the level of decomposition of the bodies, it is apparent that Sally is the surviving spouse," Charron wrote in the court filing.

Realtor.com reached out to Marchian’s lawyer, John C. Lewis III, for comment.
