📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows.
  • It has been revealed that the old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes.
  • According to recent reports, from Census: Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction.

It has been revealed that the old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021: when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%.

According to recent reports, from Census: Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October.As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a newly introduced rate hike cycle.

Industry observers note that single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive.

One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but upcoming home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the major publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product.

Latest home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the substantial builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years.

Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The massive builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more.

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.
  • On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.
  • Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

It has been revealed that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It states: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

According to recent reports, the schedule is fixed. Circle unveiled in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide indicates "message limits will tighten over time until no fresh burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

In a recent development, circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Industry observers note that funds already in transit are protected. The guide states "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small problem, but the timing makes this one more serious.

According to recent reports, many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is at the moment pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The matter lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

Currently, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

While the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

According to recent reports, once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Currently, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

It has been revealed that over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for users that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

When the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post.
  • The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:56 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multistep tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post.

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Sources indicate that google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, but significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Recent findings suggest that today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward stated that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also aims to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

According to recent reports, gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

Sources indicate that “When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other consumers,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.”.

Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the upgrade. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing.

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

According to recent reports, none could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Recent findings suggest that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He mentioned he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

According to recent reports, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be stated for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

According to recent reports, megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

It has been revealed that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he mentioned. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Recent findings suggest that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s presently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

According to recent reports, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she noted, but it highlighted cold.

According to recent reports, “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Sources indicate that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and upcoming construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Industry observers note that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova mentioned. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

According to recent reports, hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he notes, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

Recent findings suggest that he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

It has been revealed that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer noted. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

Sources indicate that she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

According to recent reports, shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, Newly introduced Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

According to recent reports, his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein noted.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

It has been revealed that “Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

In a recent development, bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova remarked she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • fix-and-flip market weakened in the third quarter as mortgage rates above 7% slowed buyer demand, while falling home prices and higher labor costs squeezed investors’ margins, according to a survey from Kiavi and John Burns Research and Consulting.
  • In a recent development, the Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index fell to a reading of 53 in the third quarter, down from 59 in the second quarter and 56 a year earlier.
  • Readings below 50 indicate market contraction, while readings above 50 indicate expansion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. fix-and-flip market weakened in the third quarter as mortgage rates above 7% slowed buyer demand, while falling home prices and higher labor costs squeezed investors’ margins, according to a survey from Kiavi and John Burns Research and Consulting.

In a recent development, the Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index fell to a reading of 53 in the third quarter, down from 59 in the second quarter and 56 a year earlier. The index, which measures market conditions on a scale of 0 to 100, reached its lowest level in nearly four years.

Readings below 50 indicate market contraction, while readings above 50 indicate expansion. The November 2026 report is based on a proprietary quarterly survey of approximately 280 fix-and-flip investors.

Recent findings suggest that only 23% of flippers expect good sales over the next six months, the lowest share in four years. Meanwhile, 19% anticipate poor sales, the highest share since Q4 2022.

Sources indicate that the slowdown is affecting investors of different sizes. Large flippers, defined as those who bought or sold at least eight homes over the previous 18 months, reported worse market conditions than smaller operators for the first time since Q3 2022.

Recent findings suggest that higher mortgage rates have also reduced pricing power for investors. Forty percent of flippers said home sale prices in their markets were lower than a year earlier, compared with 16% who reported higher prices. Another 36% said prices were largely unchanged.

It has been revealed that the Southwest reported the greatest share of flippers experiencing lower prices, at 67%, followed by Southern California at 50%. In Texas and the Southeast, 47% reported lower prices, while 44% of Florida respondents stated the same.

About one in five flippers said they were selling homes mostly below their initial after-repair value estimates, approaching the highest level recorded by the survey since 2021.

The survey also found that immigration enforcement is affecting renovation labor availability and costs. Forty-one percent of flippers mentioned increased immigration enforcement had negatively affected their labor force, up from 33% when the question was asked in Q2 2025.

Respondents reported difficulties finding workers, higher labor costs and longer project timelines. The impact was particularly pronounced in Florida and the Southeast, although flippers in other regions also reported challenges.

More available inventory is creating additional acquisition opportunities for investors. Twenty-four percent of flippers stated competition for deals was lower than usual, the highest share in the survey’s history.

Recent findings suggest that despite the increased availability, investors remain cautious about how much they’re willing to pay. The average flipper targeted a maximum purchase price of 67% of a property’s after-repair value, down slightly from the previous quarter.

Renovation costs also varied significantly by region. The national average cost per flipped home was $72,000 in the third quarter, with costs reaching $133,000 in Southern California and $86,000 in the Northeast. Costs were lower in the Southeast and Texas, at $47,000 and $46,000, respectively.

It has been revealed that the survey’s findings point to continued pressure on investors as higher financing costs, weaker buyer demand and labor constraints complicate project economics. As a result, John Burns recommended that flippers remain disciplined when acquiring properties and build in sufficient margins to account for potential price declines and higher labor expenses.

The firm also advised lenders to underwrite properties based on expected sale prices at the time of disposition rather than relying solely on recently closed comparable sales, which can lag in a declining market.

The 240 million XRP did not reach any exchange after the transfers, according to XRPSCAN data.

The drop in XRP comes amid outflows from U.S. spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds recorded net outflows of $19.13 million between Nov. 9 and Nov. 13, and it was their worst week since March 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:23 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

According to recent reports, high-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery.

Recent findings suggest that that shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC.

“We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver remarked.

Recent findings suggest that ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The organization laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements. Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik.

“You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.”.

Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up front to decide which candidates are worth testing, Ma-Weaver noted.

“What we’re seeing, for example, with computer-aided engineering, is that you can actually identify ahead of time which are non-essential parameters and you don’t run the simulation, thereby reducing the total simulation time,” she said. “We also find that if you’re doing design and you have initial prototypes, you can generate upcoming, novel and creative prototypes.”.

Sources indicate that the gains are already reaching weather forecasting in production. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s forecasting platform has heavy, tightly coupled workloads and once ran only on-premises, but it now runs on Google Cloud, Ma-Weaver explained. The National Hurricane Center also used Google’s WeatherNext model to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, Gawlik noted. But the growing reliance on AI-generated results also carries a risk for younger researchers, who may lean on machine output instead of developing critical-thinking skills, she added.

Sources indicate that “AI is still not perfect,” Gawlik remarked. “I think even though there’s an output, we call it AI slop. It could still be slop.”.

#41618. What are we so afraid of?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

What are we so afraid of?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year, I discovered I absolutely love horror movies.
  • Our fears say a lot about us and our society, and I think financial fear shapes more buyer decisions than anyone realizes.
  • In a recent development, financial fears run throughout Chapman University’s latest survey of American fears, from economic collapse to medical bills and making rent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year, I discovered I absolutely love horror movies. Through their twisted stories, we can play with our fears, project them onto the screen and laugh at them collectively. I can’t watch them alone, but I started a Scary Movie Club.

Our fears say a lot about us and our society, and I think financial fear shapes more buyer decisions than anyone realizes.

In a recent development, financial fears run throughout Chapman University’s latest survey of American fears, from economic collapse to medical bills and making rent. Not having enough money for the future ranks above public speaking, sharks and even death.

It has been revealed that firstHome IQ’s latest NextGen Homebuyer Report, “How You’re Built to Buy” found similar levels of anxiety. Two in three respondents worry their finances won’t last, and 86% report some form of financial shame.

According to recent reports, last week I hosted a financial workshop at my gym, and with all of my Scary Movie Club members, we faced our fears together. While I’ve studied the data, that night I met the ghosts and the monsters, and they explained a lot about what’s standing between buyers and their financial goals.

Industry observers note that I pitched my financial workshop at run club with promises of pizza and games. But money is still a significant scary shark in an ocean we don’t understand.

In a recent development, “Are you a psychopath?!” One run club member laughed as I excitedly shared the proposal for collectively discussing our finances. “Are you also going to tell me we’ll be public speaking after?” (He attended, and now that I think about it, I did make him public speak a little).

I discovered the level of my own horror in finance a couple of years ago when I hired a financial advisor. I smiled and nodded, with a tightened chest and shallow breath. I later noticed my fitness tracker thought my meeting was a nap. It confused my frozen, horrified body as shutting down for sleep. (The last time it recorded a nap was during The Conjuring, while we waited for the demon to inhabit the mother and I was too scared to breathe).

Since I started researching financial psychology, I have been pleasantly surprised to find out how unexceptional that financial horror is. In keynotes for housing professionals and in our financial fitness workshop, everyone has their own financial ghost story.

In a recent development, someone who grew up with very little noted that when money comes in, it still looks like a way to plug a hole. “Even though my life’s changed so much now from when I was a kid, I don’t think my brain ever stopped thinking, like, okay, plug this up, plug this up.”.

In our research, earning more and saving consistently didn’t impact the anxiety, avoidance or shame numbers by much, likely because they’re old stories. Researchers at Cambridge found that many of the habits we bring to money are largely in place by the time we’re seven, absorbed from our parents’ relationship with money.

According to recent reports, if you haven’t seen Poltergeist, the family’s dream house turns out to be built on top of a cemetery with some very active ghosts. We can make more money, save more money, and move into the nicer house, but the bodies are still down there.

For one person in the room, that history had shaped whether owning a home ever seemed like an option. “When you grow up with so little, you just really don’t think you can have those things.” By the time someone asks what they can afford, they may have already decided what kind of life is available to them.

My favorite form of financial madness is avoidance. There’s always at least one medical bill sitting on my counter, taunting me, reminding me of all the ways I fall short. Fortunately, I can afford those bills now (and usually I discover I’ve already paid them). But this is the kind of sick game we play.

Industry observers note that in our survey, over a third of people are avoiding the bill on their counter, too. One woman said of her financial anxiety, “My brain just keeps cycling through the fear instead of realizing that it’s not rational.”.

Last week, I interviewed Todd Ballenger, a professor and loan officer, on financial psychology, and he told me the fear of being judged is the number one reason people don’t call. People are afraid of being judged, of being taken advantage of, of not knowing something they should.

A business owner in our workshop mentioned of investing in property, “It’s a game I don’t fully understand…so I defer it, and I defer it.” Over half in our survey said they avoided talking with a professional because of how they might look.

Industry observers note that that fear reminded me of Brené Brown’s viral TED Talk, where she described shame as something that grows in secrecy, silence and judgment. It is the creaking staircase to the dark basement, the unknown around the corner.

Todd said we can’t focus our attention on the hardest things. “Think about where you feel the opposite of shame in your finances,” and he said to start building there.

Industry observers note that I held the workshop at my gym because it’s where we already do hard things together. I still can’t watch a horror movie by myself, and I don’t think most people can face their finances by themselves either.

Everyone has a ghost in their basement, and it’s your job to make sure they don’t go down there alone.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) has printed a death cross for the first time in 14 months on its daily chart. The 50 MA is below the 200 MA. This death cross follows the last signal, which was back in September 2025.

The latest death cross signal coincides with a sharp price drop, with Shiba Inu falling to unusually low levels below $0.000004.

Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Shiba Inu dropping sharply to a low of $0.0000037 on Saturday, marking four straight days of declines since November 11.

In a recent development, A death cross was completed on its daily chart, reflecting the ongoing selling pressure in the market. Crypto has been pummeled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors; liquidations accelerated over the last 24 hours, reaching a total of $1.96 billion across the market, according to CoinGlass data.

Unlike the abrupt crashes that have punctuated previous crypto downturns, much of the preceding decline unfolded during relatively subdued trading before liquidations accelerated in recent days.

The latest selloff is testing the resolve of some of the cryptocurrency market’s most committed investors, as a succession of setbacks pushes prices toward their lowest levels of the year and major sources of demand weaken.

Stablecoin supply is shrinking fast, dropping $17 billion over the last month, the steepest drop since 2022. As holders swap stablecoins for fiat, they drain buying power from BTC and crypto, analysts at Glassnode noted.

It remains to be seen whether buying power returns to the market. According to Bitwise CEO Matt Hougan, "There will be a big buying opportunity at some point, but it's hard to say when.".

Shiba Inu rebounded from a low of $0.0000037 on Sunday, but the meme coin remains down 6.87% over the last 24 hours and down 14% over the week.

Further recovery will occur if dip buying gains traction, with the daily 50 MA and 200 MA at $0.000005 marking resistance levels for SHIB's price. Support is expected at $0.000003 if the declines continue.

Recent findings suggest that homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

In a recent development, krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

Sources indicate that that opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

Sources indicate that the company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it states can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this significant news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

Sources indicate that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

According to recent reports, the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Recent findings suggest that proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration proposal and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

Recent findings suggest that the technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository indicates a yes vote does two things:.

It has been revealed that it also claims plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

According to recent reports, A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

In a recent development, turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Recent findings suggest that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

According to recent reports, the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC indicated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Sources indicate that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Recent findings suggest that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

It has been revealed that the spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Recent findings suggest that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

Cardano's Hoskinson States Everyone Will Be Happy Next Year

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is sending out a hopeful message to the crypto space in the wake of a brutal market crash that is causing ADA to come very close to falling out of the top 20 crypto assets.
  • Recently, Hoskinson took to X to respond to a frustrated Cardano fan who posted a screenshot showing ADA falling almost 10% in the last 24 hours.
  • “It’s all going to be ok,” said Hoskinson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is sending out a hopeful message to the crypto space in the wake of a brutal market crash that is causing ADA to come very close to falling out of the top 20 crypto assets.

Recently, Hoskinson took to X to respond to a frustrated Cardano fan who posted a screenshot showing ADA falling almost 10% in the last 24 hours.

“It’s all going to be ok,” said Hoskinson. “Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy.”.

The recent crypto market crash has proven to be extremely brutal for a lot of different assets, and Cardano is certainly one of the worst affected.

In recent trading, ADA has fallen all the way down to around $0.15.

At these levels, ADA is right now down around 95% from its all-time high of $3.09, which was reached in September 2021, based on data from CoinGecko.

This represents an almost complete loss of investment value for those who bought at the all-time high.

Overall, Cardano is also down around 35% in the last month and almost 60% since the start of 2026.

As a result, Cardano’s market cap has fallen all the way down to around $5.7 billion, with ADA dropping to 18th place in CoinGecko’s crypto rankings.

This is a very precarious position for the once-dominant altcoin Cardano, which is now extremely close to falling out of the top 20.

It seems as though there are a few different factors at play behind Cardano’s poor performance.

Industry observers note that first of all, there has been a huge sell-off in the broader crypto market. Bitcoin has seen major drops, leading to more selling pressure on major altcoins.

This decline has coincided with a falling technology stock market, ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty, outflows from crypto investment products, and mass liquidations of leveraged positions.

That mentioned, there are clearly some issues with Cardano beyond the wider market struggles.

For one, Cardano has faced a lot of criticism over the years for the blockchain’s relatively low adoption, even after years of development. This is especially evident when compared to other chains like Ethereum and Solana.

In fact, Cardano’s decentralized finance ecosystem has recently seen around $46 million in total value locked, as reported by DefiLlama.

Elsewhere, Hoskinson recently found himself embroiled in another controversy surrounding Cardano’s future.

In another recent X post, Hoskinson lashed out at certain commentators who keep bashing the blockchain for its apparent lack of adoption.

He noted that critics initially claimed Cardano suffered from poor on-chain metrics, few real-world use cases and technology that no one wanted to use.

Then, when Hoskinson decided to work on developing apps that would be able to attract millions of people and billions in assets, it seemed as though those same critics began claiming he was scamming everyone.

Sources indicate that “You people are both stupid and scum. I can’t fix stupid,” stated Hoskinson. “Grow up.”.

#41612. The housing cliff is here.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1048 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

The housing cliff is here.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, something is happening in the American housing market that should be setting off alarm bells in Washington.
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, our mortgage company was setting production records, in spite of the poor pace of existing home sales.
  • In October, our lock volume declined 51% compared to October 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, something is happening in the American housing market that should be setting off alarm bells in Washington. Yet the response from policymakers has been either remarkably misguided or mute.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, our mortgage company was setting production records, in spite of the poor pace of existing home sales. We’ve grown considerably over the past several years, expanding our reach, reducing our costs to manufacture and investing heavily in technology.

Then the market fell off a cliff. Not a seasonal slowdown. Not an understandable contraction. A cliff.

In October, our lock volume declined 51% compared to October 2025. Think about that. A tech giant that was setting records this spring, with a larger and more efficient operating platform than a year ago, experienced a 51% year-over-year collapse in locked production.

Trust me, we’re not alone. The fraternity of IMBs may be fiercely competitive, but it also understands that a falling tide lowers all boats.

It has been revealed that the Mortgage Bankers Association’s weekly Mortgage Applications Index is down 42% year over year as of October 30. Mortgage Capital Trading (MCT) reported September mortgage locks down 27.25% year over year.

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported September pending home sales declining 11.3% year over year, with its Pending Home Sales Index plunging to 66.0, the lowest reading in the index’s entire history, dating back to 2001.

But here’s the problem. Both MCT’s and NAR’s figures reflect September activity.

By the time those reports reach policymakers, lenders have already experienced October’s deterioration and are projecting November.

Sources indicate that if any other industry of this magnitude were experiencing a contraction this severe, it would dominate headlines. Legislators would be demanding answers. Industry leaders would be called to Washington. A task force would be formed, and we surely wouldn’t be talking about “considering” how to cancel mortgage insurance more proactively for loans that haven’t even closed yet. I’ve been originating for 21 years. You know how many times I’ve had a client reach out because they were having difficulty canceling PMI? Zero.

In a recent development, the warning signs come before the closings. If you’re looking at existing home sales or September’s data, you’re sitting comfortably in the caboose while the front of the train has gone over the edge.

Industry observers note that housing doesn’t begin at closing. It begins with consumer interest, credit inquiries, mortgage applications, rate locks and purchase contracts. These are our leading indicators. And they’re flashing red. When apps disappear, locks follow. When locks disappear, closings follow. And when closings disappear, the financial consequences spread across an enormous industry.

Sources indicate that downsizing has already begun. Again. These decisions are painful. But responsible leaders must act, not hope. Mortgage lenders cannot continue carrying rising healthcare costs, salaries and operating expenses into a production decline this severe, particularly as we enter the fourth and first quarters, our slowest seasons. We’ve been in a housing recession for four consecutive years. But what’s happening now is worse.

Here’s the contradiction I find most troubling.

In a recent development, while the mortgage industry contracts, the institutions charged with supporting housing finance are reporting extraordinary financial results. Fannie Mae earned $4.2 billion in the third quarter, bringing its net worth to $119.6 billion. Freddie Mac earned another $3.2 billion, with net worth reaching $81 billion.

That’s $7.4 billion in quarterly profits and more than $200 billion in combined net worth. And what is the Director saying? He’s bragging about it. Bragging.

Meanwhile, FHA’s most recent annual report showed its Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund holding $188.9 billion in capital, with an 11.47% capital ratio, more than five times the statutory minimum. FHA has never been as richly capitalized as it is today.

In a recent development, strong balance sheets are important. Taxpayers deserve protection. Nobody is suggesting we abandon prudent risk management. But how do we reconcile this financial strength with today’s housing market?

Consider this: Fannie Mae reported that more than 70% of its third-quarter guarantee-fee income came from loans and related securities issued in 2022 or earlier.

Industry observers note that the agencies can continue generating enormous earnings from their existing portfolios even as upcoming mortgage activity contracts. That’s an explanation for their profitability. It is not a justification for ignoring the affordability crisis.

In 2024, Fannie and Freddie collected an average of 65.2 basis points in g-fees on fresh single-family acquisitions.

It has been revealed that FHFA should be evaluating those fees against actual credit risk, capital requirements and the substantial recurring earnings generated by existing guarantees. Even modest, responsibly calibrated reductions could lower borrowing costs if passed through to consumers.

In a recent development, congress should repeal the 10-basis-point guarantee-fee surcharge originally imposed in 2011 to fund an unrelated payroll tax extension. If you’ve gotten a conforming loan since 2012 and you still have it, 10 basis points of your rate is going to pay for a 2-month payroll tax cut that happened 14 years ago. By the way, the CBO remarked the cut would cost $30 billion. We’ve repaid $56 billion.

These aren’t silver bullets. But they’re tangible, measurable actions that can reduce costs without abandoning responsible risk management.

In a recent development, I’m not suggesting that government agencies should sacrifice financial stability to rescue mortgage companies. I’m suggesting something far more fundamental.

According to recent reports, the success of America’s housing finance system cannot be measured solely by the profitability of the institutions that support it. It must also be measured by whether American families can afford to participate in it.

Right now, those two measurements are telling very different stories.

Washington needs to recognize what’s happening in real time, engage directly with industry leaders and take meaningful steps to improve affordability.

Because every month spent admiring backward-looking financial results is another month that businesses must downsize, housing transactions disappear and families are priced out of homeownership.

The housing cliff isn’t something we’re approaching. We’re already falling off it. And the time to act is now.

Tech Report: NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Sources indicate that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Sources indicate that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO mentioned he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

Sources indicate that white also allegedly remarked that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or blueprint.”.

Sources indicate that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Sources indicate that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears remarked the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

According to recent reports, “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” stated David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Industry observers note that pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

#41610. Six days, six outages: Why reliability isn’t resilience

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2202 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Six days, six outages: Why reliability isn’t resilience

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • A rash of major outages over the past week all seem to follow a similar script.
  • Recent findings suggest that none of these was a cyberattack, and as far as anyone can tell, none was related.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:21 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

A rash of major outages over the past week all seem to follow a similar script. Services go dark, Downdetector lights up, the provider posts a string of status updates, a root cause emerges a few days later, and everyone goes back to work, assuming it won’t happen again. This past week, that script was on overdrive.

Recent findings suggest that none of these was a cyberattack, and as far as anyone can tell, none was related. A dormant bug, overloaded legacy routers, a bad internal enhancement and an on-premises hardware glitch are about as different as root causes get. Some of these systems run in the public cloud, some in a tech giant’s own data center, and some on air traffic control gear that’s decades old. That’s precisely the point. The common thread isn’t the technology. It’s that each organization had a critical dependency fail, and the business stopped with it.

It has been revealed that that’s the lesson I want business leaders to take away. Outages aren’t rare events to be explained away after the fact. They’re a certainty to plan for, and the plan must address what happens when an entire service fails, not just a server or a data center.

I wanted to dig into what real resilience looks like, and Zscaler Inc. is an interesting case study for a specific reason. When a company deploys Zscaler, every user, branch and device connects to applications through its Zero Trust Exchange. That places Zscaler squarely in the critical path. If it goes down, users can’t reach Microsoft 365, Salesforce, internal apps or anything else, no matter how healthy those applications are. That all-or-nothing exposure has forced Zscaler to think harder than most about what happens when its service fails.

At the last Zenith Live, Zscaler’s user event, I asked Chief Executive Jay Chaudhry about this, and he explained that because of the critical nature of their offering, it can’t afford any downtime, so the manufacturer built resiliency into its service design. After all these outages, I asked to speak with Chaudhry and Chief Reliability Officer Misha Kuperman to gather lessons learned for the industry.

It has been revealed that to be clear, Zscaler couldn’t have kept a single Microsoft mailbox online or restarted the FAA’s routers, and no one at the organization claimed otherwise. But its approach to continuity for its own platform is a useful model for how any service on a company’s critical path, including software-as-a-service, should be architected. Here are my thoughts on what this means for boards and C-suite leaders:.

Sources indicate that I came from financial services, where the disaster recovery site was non-negotiable and everyone knew which services had to survive a failure. Chaudhry, who spent years at IBM Corp., made the same point.

It has been revealed that “Most of my large customers had a production data center and a DR data center,” he told me. “If the production data center went down, they’d fail over to DR. That was standard practice. When the world moved to the cloud, they forgot about it, thinking disaster recovery was the cloud provider’s responsibility, even though it is actually a shared responsibility.”.

It has been revealed that he’s right, and the record proves it. Availability zones and multiregion designs protect against hardware failures and localized events, but they share software, control planes, configuration pipelines and often DNS. When a bad configuration or a dormant bug propagates, it spreads everywhere. That’s exactly what happened to Microsoft.

Availability architecture and resilience architecture aren’t the same thing. One keeps a service up when a component fails. The other keeps the business running when the entire service fails. Most companies have the first and assume they have the second, but as we have seen recently, that assumption is incorrect.

During the call, Chaudhry used an analogy that everyone can understand. You can own the world’s most reliable car and service it religiously, yet you still buy insurance for other risks not covered by the warranty, such as theft or a tree falling on it. Having insurance and knowing when and how to use it helps you get back on the road quickly. Zscaler has built the cyber equivalent.

Recent findings suggest that in the real world, people understand it. In cyber and digital, we seem to forget and rely on service-level agreements. A 99.999% uptime commitment sounds good until you translate it into business terms. Chaudhry stated some of Zscaler’s largest banking customers told the organization that five nines wasn’t enough, “because we could lose hundreds of millions of dollars if you went down even for five minutes.”.

Going back to my IT days, I’ve never liked SLAs because they are financial instruments, not operational ones. They tell you what credit you’ll receive after the fact, not how you’ll keep processing payments, as Chase customers learned, or how you’ll keep planes in the air, as United learned. Regulators have recognized this. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and Australia’s CPS 230 both require regulated firms to assess, test, and mitigate the risk posed by their technology providers. “Our cloud provider went down” is no longer an acceptable defense.

IT executives should stop asking, “What’s our provider’s SLA?” and start asking, “What must our business continue to do when a critical dependency fails, and have we proven we can do so?”.

Recent findings suggest that the instinctive response to an outage like Microsoft’s is to buy from a second provider. Chaudhry shared a story about a chief information officer whose CEO had flagged Office 365 as a business risk and told him to find an alternative. The CIO signed up for Google Workspace. When asked whether documents, links and role-based access controls would work after a switch, even in half the cases, he said he didn’t think so.

According to recent reports, that’s the reality. Email alone is hard enough because users lose their history the moment they switch. Modern productivity suites aren’t storage anymore. Every email includes links to shared documents, permissions are tied to identity, and workflows span multiple apps. Kuperman framed the problem in terms of scale: “I can switch between Gmail and Outlook, but can 10,000 people? Will they be as productive?”.

The same problem applies in security and networking, where the stakes are arguably higher. The vendor A/vendor B model requires two policy sets kept in perfect sync, two client software sets and a way to move tens of thousands of customers and devices from one to the other in the middle of a crisis. Kuperman described one customer for whom it “used to take seven days to switch over and 30 days to switch back. You can’t run a business like that.”.

According to recent reports, A backup that’s never tested at full scale isn’t a backup. It’s a hope. And a backup that changes the user experience will fail exactly when it’s needed.

Recent findings suggest that another instinct is to turn off security entirely; however, when a crisis occurs, threat actors will rally and launch campaigns. During the CrowdStrike outage, phishing campaigns were mobilized almost immediately, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency had to problem warnings not to take the bait. Threat actors are present both internally and externally, so security must remain on guard during critical failures, especially when they are publicly known.

This brings me to what Zscaler has done with its Business Continuity Cloud and why I think it’s the right template for the industry. Rather than asking customers to bolt on a second vendor, Zscaler built a dedicated, per-customer environment that’s architecturally separate from its primary Zero Trust Exchange.

Sources indicate that the design choices are important to understand. The Business Continuity Cloud runs in third-party data centers, not Zscaler’s own, on separate networks, autonomous system numbers, DNS, and cloud domains. Software and threat-intelligence updates are deliberately staggered so a bad production release can’t land in the backup at the same time. Policy and identity data sync one way into a read-only, last-known-good state. It’s offered across nine regions, enough to keep operations in-country if a nation were cut off.

Sources indicate that “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry noted. That’s the old production/DR discipline, rebuilt for the cloud. After watching overloaded routers ground the nation’s air traffic, “no shared routers” doesn’t sound like overkill.

There were two operational details I felt were worth noting. First, Zscaler encourages customers to continuously route synthetic or trusted-user traffic through the backup environment in peacetime, so the failover path is validated daily rather than in an annual tabletop exercise. Second, the failover is automated to optimize for a low recovery time objective or RTO, or it can be triggered by the customer, ensuring it works even if Zscaler itself is unreachable.

Industry observers note that zscaler says nearly 100 customers now use its service, including a global bank with more than 300,000 people, a global pharmaceutical firm with more than 100,000, and a U.S. telco with more than 75,000. The company charges what Chaudhry called a nominal fee to cover the dedicated infrastructure, network and always-on capacity.

The lesson from the Microsoft outage, in particular, isn’t that customers need a second productivity suite. It’s that the primary provider should offer a fate-separated continuity environment as part of the service. Zscaler has shown it can be done for a global security cloud. I’d like to see every SaaS provider that sits in a tech giant’s critical path, and Microsoft in particular, be pressed by large customers to offer the same.

According to recent reports, the Microsoft outage also exposed a concentration risk that many companies have faced through enterprise licensing agreements. Microsoft noted the incident affected not only Exchange and Teams but also Defender XDR, Defender for Office 365 and Intune. For many organizations, Microsoft is the productivity suite, the identity provider and the security stack. When the shared infrastructure beneath them fails, all three can fail together.

In a recent development, kuperman described the minimum set of capabilities a business needs to keep operating during a disaster: people, identity, network and security, and business-critical applications. Each must work, and any one can fail. “You have to think about where your eggs are and which baskets they’re in,” he said.

In a recent development, I’m not arguing against platforms. But boards should understand where consolidation has created a single point of failure across identity, applications and security, and ensure those layers don’t share the same fate.

This won’t be the last major outage, and the next one may be a cyberattack, a war, or a configuration push rather than a dormant bug. Here’s what I recommend IT and business leaders do now:.

Industry observers note that the cloud delivered on its promise of agility and scale, but in the process, the industry let a hard-won discipline lapse. This past week reminded us that everything fails eventually, whether in the cloud, a data center or an air traffic control tower. When it does, an SLA credit won’t keep the business running. A real continuity blueprint will.

Industry observers note that zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
